item.title: Spring Cloud 2026.0.0-RC2 (aka Paddington) Has Been Released
item.dc:creator: ryanjbaxter
item.content:encoded:
On behalf of the community, I am pleased to announce that the Release Candidate 2 (RC2) of the Spring Cloud 2026.0.0-RC2 Release Train is available today. The release can be found in the Spring milestone repository. You can check out the 2026.0.0-RC2 release notes for more information.

Notable Changes in the 2026.0.0-RC2 Release Train

This release is based on Spring Boot 4.2.0-RC2.

A complete list of changes can be found in the project board on GitHub.

Spring Cloud Config

  • Google Cloud Storage now supported as a backend of the Config Server (#3343)
  • Plain text and binary files can now be fetched from the Config Server as a Resource (#3355)

Spring Cloud Gateway

  • Add LocalResponseCache filter to Spring Cloud Gateway Server Web MVC (#4249)

Spring Cloud Openfeign

  • Send the nested objects of @SpringQueryMap as nested query parameters (#1448)

The following modules were updated as part of 2026.0.0-RC2:

Module Version Issues
Spring Cloud Build 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Circuitbreaker 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Commons 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Config 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Consul 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Function 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Gateway 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Kubernetes 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Netflix 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Openfeign 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Starter Build 2026.0.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Stream 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Task 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Vault 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)
Spring Cloud Zookeeper 5.1.0-RC2 (issues)

As always, we welcome feedback on GitHub, on Gitter, on Stack Overflow, or on Twitter.

To get started with Maven with a BOM (dependency management only):

<properties>
    <spring-cloud.version>2026.0.0-RC2</spring-cloud.version>
</properties>
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>${spring-cloud.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-config</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    ...
</dependencies>

or with Gradle:

plugins {
  id 'java'
  id 'org.springframework.boot' version '4.2.0-RC2'
  id 'io.spring.dependency-management' version '1.1.7'
}

repositories {
  mavenCentral()
}

ext {
  set('springCloudVersion', "2026.0.0-RC2")
}

dependencies {
  implementation 'org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-config'
  implementation 'org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client'
}

dependencyManagement {
  imports {
    mavenBom "org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-dependencies:${springCloudVersion}"
  }
}

item.title: A Bootiful Podcast: Temporal.io's Cornelia Davis
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! In this nostalgic, wide-ranging conversation, I revisit my first podcast episode from 2018 with Cornelia Davis and catch up on her career across Pivotal, VMware, Weaveworks, Amazon, Kubernetes, and now Temporal. I reflect on the enduring relevance of cloud-native patterns, workflow engines, and the evolution of software delivery from infrastructure-centric systems to durable execution.

Cornelia explains Temporal in depth: an open-source platform for long-running, stateful, asynchronous workflows that preserves execution history so processes can resume exactly where they left off, even after failures or long waits. We cover human-in-the-loop workflows, event sourcing, multi-language SDKs, open source versus cloud, and why Temporal is especially well suited for modern AI and agentic applications. She also highlights the Temporal Agent Harness, strong typing, policy-based approvals, and use cases ranging from enterprise processes to OpenAI-scale agent infrastructure.

I close the episode with practical pointers for learning more through Temporal’s website, blog, community resources, and GitHub, plus Cornelia’s preferred online presence on LinkedIn.

#temporal #ai #workflows #engineering #pivotal #agents #harnesses #durableexecution

item.title: This Week in Spring - November 3rd, 2026
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! Welcome to another installment of This Week in Spring! It's Tuesday, and you know what that means? I'm thinking about production. Now, to be fair, I'm always thinking about production. But recently, I've been spending the weekend just overjoyed at how simple it was to get Cloud Foundry working on my laptop, in Docker, with this GitHub repository. You see, I normally rely on an internal cluster at work to try out the latest and greatest in the platform, but I've always wanted to run the whole thing locally. It's like four steps. But don't even do those steps. Instead, just launch your favorite AI and point it to the instructions. You'll just need to have Docker and kind running on your host, and your AI agent will take care of the rest. I used Claude, but you do you. Why do I mention this? I love Cloud Foundry. It's like if you took the ideals of Spring Boot and applied them to a platform where your applications run. Strong opinions, loosely held. The platform and the framework, combined, let me focus on the important stuff: getting to production.

You wanna try it out? Why not!

First, install Cloud Foundry in kind as explained above.

Second, install the cf CLI.

  • on macOS:
brew install cloudfoundry/tap/cf-cli@8
  • on Windows:
# Using Chocolatey
choco install cloudfoundry-cli

# Or using Winget
winget install CloudFoundry.cli
  • on Linux, you can probably just use your distro's package manager and, failing that, use this:

curl -L "https://packages.cloudfoundry.org/stable?release=linux64-binary&version=v8&source=github" | tar -zx

# Move to your path
sudo mv cf8 /usr/local/bin/cf8
sudo mv cf /usr/local/bin/cf

Third, build a Spring Boot application. Hit the Spring Initializr and create a new application using Java 17, and add Web. Here's what I put at the bottom of my DemoApplication class:

@Controller
@ResponseBody
class HelloController {

	@GetMapping("/")
	Map<String, String> hello() {
		return Map.of("name", "Hello, Cloud Foundry!");
	}
}

Then in the command line:

./mvnw package && cd target && cf push -p *jar myapp

After 30 seconds or so, it'll be done and you can interrogate the application with:

cf applications

TIP: you could also use cf a as an alias for cf applications.

You'll see the URL of the application in the output. Bring up the application and you're off to the races!

Anyway, enough chit-chat about my new obsession... let's dive into this week's roundup!

  • guess what: we're back with yet another amazing recipe from Craig Walls, looking at rendering rich UIs with MCP applications
  • and another one, too: speeding up RAG with faster embeddings
  • Spring Boot 3.5 is out of support: a practical, step-by-step Spring Boot 4 migration guide
  • I love Michael Redlich's amazing new Spring News roundup
  • a nice article on ADT Mag: Spring Boot 4.2 release candidate targets startup performance upgrade checks
  • our friend Siva has a nice post on harness engineering for Java and Spring Boot applications, too
  • I really enjoyed his video on spec-driven development, too

item.title: A Bootiful Podcast: 'Data Geekery' with JOOQ creator Lukas Eder
item.dc:creator: joshlong
item.content:encoded:
Hi, Spring fans! In this conversation, Josh Long explores how JOOQ turns SQL into a type-safe, fluent Java language—making complex database work safer, cleaner, and far more expressive. They cover everything from dynamic SQL transformation and cross-dialect support to low-level security, stored procedures, views, and the realities of working with modern databases like DuckDB, ClickHouse, Redshift, and more.

Along the way, Lucas reflects on the origins of JOOQ, why he built it, and how the project has evolved from a clever Java DSL into a serious platform for enterprise-grade database development. The discussion also touches on AI-assisted debugging, the enduring relevance of SQL, and how strong typing can dramatically reduce mental overhead for developers and DBAs alike.

If you care about databases, Java, or writing better software with less friction, this episode is a masterclass in thoughtful engineering and pragmatic elegance.
